choices.text: Assign 18A or 22F outbound and 17F or 23A return; if one disappears, use another no-fee window before considering aisles.
Assign 10C outbound and 9D return to keep her nearer the front on both flights.
Pay for preferred forward windows on both legs so she is both forward and by the window.
Leave seats unassigned and handle the request at airport check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: the prompt alone makes forward aisle seats plausible for deplaning, but prior trip resolutions point to free windows when seat selection is available and no competing seating need is present.
probes.gold_action: Assign no-fee standard window seats on both legs, with another free window as the fallback.
probes.label_rationale: Across earlier solo work bookings, Kara accepted no-fee windows when selection was open. With no paid-seat need or companion seating issue here, the free standard windows beat forward aisles, paid preferred seats, or waiting.
probes.query: Kara has selected a Tampa-to-Cleveland round trip for a solo pediatric tone workshop. The fare is Main Cabin and both legs have standard no-fee seat maps open. No current message mentions seat placement. Outbound free seats include 10C aisle, 18A, 22F, and 24B; return free seats include 9D aisle, 17F, 23A, and 21B. Preferred seats cost extra and are not needed for timing. What seat instruction should go into checkout?

choices.text: Move her to 14A outbound and 19A or 20F returning, using free standard windows while they are open.
Move her to 13C outbound and 11C returning because both are standard aisles with easier deplaning.
Keep the current hold without assigning seats until check-in, in case better rows appear.
Use 15D outbound and 23D returning because they are comparable standard aisle seats on both flights.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: many travelers would reasonably favor the front aisle on a generic booking page, but Kara's prior solo flight choices consistently resolve this kind of seat-map tie toward windows.
probes.gold_action: Update the hold with free standard window seats on both flights.
probes.label_rationale: Kara previously chose named window seats or asked to grab windows on solo clinic and course trips. Since the listed windows are free and timing is not at stake, select them rather than defaulting to aisles.
probes.query: The airline seat map for Kara's solo Tampa-to-Cincinnati pediatric spasticity lab trip has opened after the flight hold. Both flights are regular economy and all listed seats are free standard seats. On the outbound, 14A, 26F, 13C aisle, and 15D aisle are open. On the return, 11C aisle is closest to the front, and 19A, 20F, and 23D aisle are open. She has not given a new seat note. Which update should be made?

choices.text: Pick 19A or 20F on the first leg and 18F on the second leg, keeping no-fee windows first.
Pick 8C and 7D to deplane a few rows sooner during the connection.
Skip assignments and add a note to ask at the gate if better seats open.
Pick an aisle only on the first leg because of the connection, then use 18F on the second leg.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the connection makes forward aisle seats a credible query-only answer, but the connection is not tight enough to trigger one of Kara's seat-location exceptions.
probes.gold_action: Assign free standard window seats on both segments despite the ordinary connection.
probes.label_rationale: Past solo clinic and seminar bookings use windows when maps allow. A normal same-terminal connection is not enough to override that with aisles on otherwise comparable free seats.
probes.query: Kara is ticketing a solo Tampa-to-Fort Wayne pediatric bracing clinic visit. The itinerary has a 68-minute same-terminal connection, regular economy, and no checked bags; all listed seats are standard and no-fee. First leg seats include 8C aisle, 19A window, and 20F window. Second leg seats include 7D aisle, 18F window, and 22C aisle. No new seat instruction appears in the thread. Which seat plan should be entered?

choices.text: Take 20B/20C together and set a reminder to look for a free window-adjacent pair later.
Put Kara in 15A and Dan in 24F so both have no-fee windows.
Buy 9A/9B so Kara can have a window while they sit together.
Assign Kara 15A and leave Dan unassigned until check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the paid adjacent window pair is a realistic upgrade, but prior partner-seat handling favors adjacent free seating unless a current note says to spend for the window.
probes.gold_action: Keep the travelers adjacent in the free standard pair and monitor for a free window-adjacent improvement.
probes.label_rationale: On partner trips, Kara repeatedly put staying together ahead of her window seat when both could not be satisfied cheaply. The no-fee adjacent pair with a later seat check follows that pattern.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are booking a Tampa-to-Greenville weekend flight on one reservation. The fare includes standard seats. The only no-fee adjacent pair left is 20B/20C; separate no-fee windows are 15A and 24F. A preferred 9A/9B pair costs $92 total. The booking page allows paid seats, but the current thread is silent on seat upgrades. What should the planner do?

choices.text: Keep 18A on the long leg; assign 16C on the short leg and set a check-in reminder for a free window.
Pay $48 for the short-leg window so every leg has the same seat location.
Keep 18A on the long leg; assign 22D on the short leg and take no further seat action.
Leave the short leg unassigned and rely on the gate to place her.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the usual seat location points toward the paid window, while the fee, short segment, and prior paid-seat exceptions point toward a free non-middle seat plus a later try.
probes.gold_action: Use the best free non-middle seat on the short segment and set a reminder to try for a free window later.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has declined paid windows on individual segments and used a free non-middle seat or a check-in reminder instead. The short fee-only window is not enough reason to buy an upgrade.
probes.query: On Kara's solo Tampa-to-Des Moines clinic-training itinerary, the long outbound leg already has no-fee 18A. The short return connection is 54 minutes in the air; its only remaining window is a $48 preferred seat, while free standard seats include 16C aisle, 18B middle, and 22D aisle. The current thread is silent on seat upgrades. What seat action should go in the booking?

choices.text: Use the free 18C/18D adjacent pair on the return and watch for a free adjacent window pair.
Split them into 21A and 24F so each traveler has a free window.
Pay for 8A/8B because it is the only adjacent pair with a window.
Put Kara in 21A and her partner in 18C so at least one traveler has a window.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: a paid adjacent window pair would satisfy both seat location and togetherness, but the past partner-trip tradeoff rejects that cost when a workable free adjacent pair exists.
probes.gold_action: Keep the return seats adjacent and free, while monitoring for a no-fee adjacent window option.
probes.label_rationale: For partner returns, Kara favors adjacent/free seats over paying only for a window. Keep them together and monitor for a free improvement instead of splitting them or buying a paid pair.
probes.query: Kara and her partner are on a Monday return from a coastal recovery weekend. Outbound seats are already together with Kara at a no-fee window. For the return, the seat map shows a free adjacent pair at 18C/18D across the aisle, separate free windows at 21A and 24F, and one adjacent window pair 8A/8B for $78 total. The current thread is silent on paid seat upgrades. What should be confirmed?

choices.text: Ticket the chosen itinerary, enter a window request for the outbound with a check-in reminder, and assign 22A on the return.
Switch to the later backup routing solely because both of its seat maps are visible now.
Ticket the chosen itinerary, assign 13C on the return, and make no outbound location request.
Ticket the chosen itinerary, pay for 6F on the return, and leave the outbound to check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the backup with visible seats is a credible generic choice, but Kara's prior handling is to request and revisit window seats when selection is deferred, not to rebuild an otherwise good itinerary.
probes.gold_action: Book the chosen itinerary, request a window where the map is closed, set a check-in reminder, and assign the free return window.
probes.label_rationale: When seat maps are open, Kara asks for windows; when not open, she treats that as a limitation to revisit. The chosen schedule should be ticketed with a request and reminder rather than changed just for visible maps.
probes.query: Kara is ready to buy a solo Tampa-to-Reno university lab itinerary that otherwise matches the host schedule. The fare includes a seat-location request, but the operating carrier will not show the outbound seat map until online check-in. The return seat map is open now with free 13C aisle, 22A window, 24D aisle, and a $35 preferred 6F window. A backup routing at the same fare arrives 25 minutes later with a longer connection and visible no-fee windows. No current message gives a new seat instruction. Which checkout note should be used?

choices.text: Buy Main Cabin and assign the open standard window seats.
Buy Basic Economy to save $31 and accept gate-assigned seats.
Buy Main Cabin but choose 12C and 18C aisle seats to keep her nearer the front.
Hold both fare types and ask whether she cares about seats on this trip.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: this is not a pure seat-map choice; it requires carrying the seat-selection pattern into a small fare tradeoff without treating price savings as automatically decisive.
probes.gold_action: Select Main Cabin and assign the available standard window seats.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has avoided random-seat fares and asked for Main Cabin windows when selection is part of booking. Saving $31 is plausible from the query alone, but it gives up current seat control.
probes.query: Kara's solo Tampa-to-Lexington pediatric lab flights are otherwise narrowed to one schedule. At checkout, Basic Economy is $31 less but says seats are assigned at the gate; Main Cabin is the same routing and includes immediate standard seat choice, with 12A and 19F open outbound and 18A open returning. The current thread does not mention a seat change or an order to take the cheapest fare. What should be selected?

choices.text: Move her to 21A outbound and 18F return, and note that both are standard no-fee seats.
Use 11C and 9D because they are closer to the front after the schedule change.
Keep the system-assigned seats and wait for check-in to see whether better seats open.
Use 21A outbound but 9D return to improve deplaning on the way home.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: schedule changes often make travelers preserve convenient forward seats, but Kara's prior changed-flight handling specifically points to restoring windows when decent free ones remain.
probes.gold_action: Move Kara back into free standard window seats on both reissued flights.
probes.label_rationale: After schedule changes, Kara has asked to be moved back to windows when available. Here both replacement windows are free, so use them rather than forward aisles or waiting.
probes.query: A schedule change on Kara's solo Tampa-to-Grand Junction pediatric course reissued her seats. The flights themselves still work, and all current options are no-fee standard seats. The outbound now offers 11C aisle, 21A window, and 25D aisle; the return offers 9D aisle, 18F window, and 22B middle. There is no new message about sitting forward or taking aisle seats. What update should be made?

choices.text: 12:10 p.m. nonstop, arriving Tampa around 2:15 p.m.; fastest home but with the tightest airport buffer.
2:45 p.m. nonstop, arriving Tampa around 4:55 p.m.; leaves a comfortable post-lab airport buffer.
6:20 p.m. one-stop, arriving Tampa around 10:25 p.m.; $28 cheaper than the 2:45 option.
8:00 a.m. Monday nonstop, arriving Tampa around 10:05 a.m.; requires another hotel night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the noon nonstop is faster and generically defensible, while the evening option is cheaper; the narrower distinction is that Kara usually leads with a comfortable afternoon return.
probes.label_rationale: Prior returns after teaching and conference trips repeatedly kept a reasonable afternoon homebound near the top when event timing allowed it. The 2:45 return fits without forcing a tight departure, late-night arrival, or extra hotel night.
probes.query: Kara is comparing Tampa-to-Cincinnati round-trip flights for a two-day pediatric feeding workshop. The Sunday hands-on lab ends at 10:45 a.m.; CVG is about 25 minutes away, the hotel can hold bags, and she has carry-on only. The outbound is fixed. The listed returns are regular economy, same carrier family, and within $45 of each other. Which return should lead the shortlist?

choices.text: 10:15 a.m. departure with one connection, arriving Tampa around 2:10 p.m.; it cuts off a relaxed morning.
1:35 p.m. departure with one connection, arriving Tampa around 5:20 p.m.; it leaves a normal morning and gets them home before evening is late.
7:05 p.m. departure with one connection, arriving Tampa just before midnight; it is $36 cheaper.
8:20 a.m. Tuesday departure, arriving Tampa around noon; it adds one more hotel night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: getting home earlier is a reasonable generic answer, but prior partner-weekend handling gives more weight to a relaxed afternoon return when no current constraint demands the morning.
probes.gold_action: Put the 1:35 p.m. Monday return first.
probes.label_rationale: Partner-weekend returns often preserve a reasonable afternoon departure rather than a rushed morning or late-night option. The 1:35 return is the closest match while avoiding an extra night.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are planning the Monday return from a Tampa-to-Traverse City recovery weekend. Checkout can be handled any time after 8:00 a.m., lunch is flexible, and there is no fixed Tampa commitment Monday evening. All choices are regular economy and within a small fare band. Which return should be first in the draft?

choices.text: 10:55 a.m. departure with one connection, arriving Tampa around 3:30 p.m.; earliest workable same-day option.
2:25 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa around 4:45 p.m.; leaves a comfortable gap after wrap-up.
7:10 p.m. departure with one connection, arriving Tampa around 11:20 p.m.; about $42 less than the 2:25 option.
6:15 a.m. Monday departure, arriving Tampa around 10:05 a.m.; adds an overnight after the seminar.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium-hard: the earliest same-day return is feasible and could appeal on a generic itinerary, but the recurring trip-resolution pattern favors the later afternoon departure when schedule and cost stay reasonable.
probes.label_rationale: For work trips with a morning wrap-up, Kara's prior choices lean to a comfortable afternoon return instead of the first possible or late-cheapest flight. The 2:25 leg best transfers that pattern here.
probes.query: Kara is comparing returns for a Tampa-to-Louisville pediatric wheelchair-seating seminar. Sunday checkout is done before the 9:30 a.m. wrap-up, SDF is about 20 to 25 minutes from the venue, and all same-day options are regular economy and within policy. Which return leg should the planner place first?
